title: The Thread That Caught Her: Charlottenburg to the Andes by way of Dessau and a Mountain in Carolina
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Charlottenburg, and the Thread She Did Not Want

stops.name: Charlottenburg, Berlin: the birth into two fortunes
stops.date_confidence: attested; 12 June 1899 and Charlottenburg confirmed by both the German and English records
stops.campa: Annelise Fleischmann is born in Charlottenburg on the twelfth of June, into a household whose money arrives from two directions. Her father, Siegfried Fleischmann, manufactures furniture. Her mother, Toni, is a daughter of Leopold Ullstein, whose presses print the newspapers of the capital. The German record writes her middle name Else and the English record writes it Elsa, and no source reached here settles which is hers. The family is Jewish and assimilated. She grows up in a house furnished by one family business and papered with the newspapers of the other.
suggested_refs: The Ullstein publishing house of Berlin, her mother's family firm
Charlottenburg civil register, birth of 12 June 1899

stops.name: Berlin: the studio of Martin Brandenburg
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: At seventeen she is set to painting under Martin Brandenburg, an Impressionist who takes private students in Berlin, and this is the whole of her formal art training before the Bauhaus. She paints portraits. Tradition holds that Oskar Kokoschka, shown one of them, asks her only why she paints, and that the question closes the studio behind her. The story reaches this account through a Wikipedia narrative with no citation attached; whether Kokoschka said it, and in which year, no source reached will confirm. She keeps painting for three more years.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Oskar Kokoschka, addressed to Anni Albers on being shown one of her portraits; reported in the Wikipedia narrative without a citation, underlying biography not opened [R]
suggested_refs: Martin Brandenburg's Berlin teaching studio
Nicholas Fox Weber, 'Anni Albers: A Life' (not opened for this account)

stops.name: Hamburg: two months at Am Lerchenfeld
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown and defaulted to January; the building is the Kunstgewerbeschule at Am Lerchenfeld 2, in use from 1913
stops.campa: She enrolls at the Staatliche Kunstgewerbeschule in Hamburg, in the brick building on Am Lerchenfeld raised just before the war, and leaves after roughly two months. The sources record the two months and not the reason. No source reached names a teacher there, a class, or a piece of work. It is the second school she has walked out of in three years. The next one refuses her first application, admits her on the second, and holds her for eleven years, and she leaves it with a trade she had not asked for.
suggested_refs: The Kunstgewerbeschule building at Am Lerchenfeld 2, Hamburg, today the Hochschule fur bildende Kunste
sources: Wikipedia, 'University of Fine Arts of Hamburg'

segments.name: Weimar: the Vorkurs and the Loom

stops.name: Weimar: the second application
stops.date_confidence: April 1922 attested; canonical Weimar Bauhaus pin inherited from itten.journey.json and paul_klee.journey.json
stops.campa: She applies to the Staatliches Bauhaus at Weimar and is refused. She applies again, and in April 1922 she is admitted, twenty-two years old, into a school three years running and already famous for what it promises: the wall, the window, the chair and the cloth all remade by the same hand. Georg Muche presides over the weaving workshop. Johannes Itten, in the school since October 1919, runs the preliminary course through which every entrant passes. Some accounts move the first rejection to another school; the German and English records both place it here.
suggested_refs: The Bauhaus admissions files, Weimar, 1921 and 1922

stops.name: Weimar: Itten's preliminary course and the Mazdaznan table
stops.date_confidence: inferred; she passes through the Vorkurs in 1922, Itten runs it 1919-1923, no month attested. Pin inherited from itten.journey.json
stops.campa: In the Vorkurs Johannes Itten teaches material by contrast: rough against smooth, hard against soft, the hand learning a surface before the eye has a name for it. He also keeps a Mazdaznan community inside the school, with its fasting, its breathing exercises, its garlic and its ranking of students by spiritual fitness. Anni Fleischmann passes through both the discipline and the cult in the year before Itten breaks with Walter Gropius and goes. The paired opposites reappear fifteen years later as her own teaching language, in an essay she writes at Black Mountain listing rough and smooth, dull and shiny, hard and soft.
suggested_refs: Itten's Vorkurs material studies, Weimar
The Mazdaznan diet sheets circulated in the Bauhaus canteen

stops.name: Weimar: the weaving workshop assigned
stops.date_confidence: [R] the steering into weaving is widely repeated in Bauhaus scholarship and the institutional mechanism is disputed; the month is a placeholder within 1922
stops.campa: She asks for the glass workshop, or for painting on walls. The Bauhaus, which declares itself open to women and in practice sends them to the loom, puts her in the weaving workshop, where most of the school's female intake goes. The mechanism is described differently in different accounts and is nowhere documented as written policy; the outcome is not in question. She learns the loom against her own preference, and she does not leave it again until she is seventy and has given the looms away.
stops.quote: In my case it was threads that caught me, really against my will. To work with threads seemed sissy to me. I wanted something to be conquered. But circumstances held me to threads and they won me over.
stops.quote_source: Anni Albers, 'Material as Metaphor' (1982), relayed with citation through the Wikipedia article 'Anni Albers'; not checked against the Wesleyan printing [A at second hand]
suggested_refs: The Bauhaus weaving workshop at Weimar under Georg Muche

stops.name: Weimar: Klee on the theory of form
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Klee is a Form Master from 1921 and she is a student from 1922, no dated encounter attested
stops.campa: Paul Klee, appointed a Form Master in 1921, teaches the theory of form to the whole student body, weaving students included, and the weavers take from him what the painters take: a way of building a surface out of intervals rather than out of pictures. Accounts of her Bauhaus years name Klee as the teacher who mattered most to her, though this account cannot produce the statement in her own words. In Dessau he becomes her neighbour. In 1933 he is dismissed and gone to Bern, and the politics that removes him puts her on a ship.
suggested_refs: Klee's form-theory notebooks from the Weimar years

segments.name: Dessau: Cellophane and the Weaving Workshop

stops.name: Dessau: the glass building and the marriage
stops.date_confidence: 1925 attested for both the move and the marriage; the day and month often given as 9 May are unsupported and duplicate her date of death, so the month defaults to January
stops.campa: The school moves to Dessau, into the glass-walled building Walter Gropius has raised for it, and in the same year she marries Josef Albers, eleven years her senior, a former schoolmaster from Westphalia who came up through the glass workshop and now teaches the preliminary course himself. She becomes Anni Albers. They will work in the same house for the next fifty-one years, and every school that employs either of them after 1933 will be in another country.
suggested_refs: The Bauhaus Dessau building by Walter Gropius, opened December 1926

stops.name: Dessau: the masters' houses on the Ebertallee
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period; month unknown and defaulted to January. Pin inherited byte-identical from paul_klee.journey.json
stops.campa: The Alberses take rooms in the masters' houses on the Ebertallee, the white cubes Gropius built for his faculty in a stand of pines. Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky share the double house next door. Josef Albers takes over the half that Laszlo Moholy-Nagy vacates in 1928. Gropius resigns the directorship in the same year, and the tenants change around her. For four years she lives on a street of painters and works in the one medium the school still classes as a trade.
suggested_refs: The Meisterhauser, Ebertallee 65-71, Dessau

stops.name: Dessau: the diploma cloth for Bernau
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia dates the diploma work 1929/30; English sources give 1929 flatly. Month unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: Her diploma work is a wall covering for the auditorium of the Bundesschule of the Allgemeiner Deutscher Gewerkschaftsbund at Bernau: cotton, linen, bast and cellophane, woven so that one face throws light back into the room and the other swallows sound. It is a functional answer to an architectural problem, arrived at on a loom. The Bernau building's own record credits Margaretha Reichardt with textiles used in its furnishings; the two commissions are described separately in the sources and are not reconciled here.
suggested_refs: The ADGB Bundesschule at Bernau bei Berlin, Meyer and Wittwer, 1928-1930
Surviving samples of the cellophane wall covering

stops.name: Dessau: one semester at the head of the workshop
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia gives autumn 1931 and one semester as interim director; accounts saying she ran the workshop until the closure are wrong, since Lilly Reich takes it in 1932
stops.campa: Gunta Stolzl, the loom master who made the workshop what it is, is forced out by student agitation against her politics and her marriage. Anni Albers takes the workshop as interim director for a single semester in the autumn. In 1932 Lilly Reich is appointed over the textile workshop and Albers is a teacher again. Stolzl had spent a season in 1923 at Johannes Itten's Ontos weaving and carpet workshops at Herrliberg on Lake Zurich, founded the year Itten left the Bauhaus.
suggested_refs: Gunta Stolzl's dismissal file, Bauhaus Dessau, 1931
The Ontos workshops at Herrliberg

stops.name: Berlin-Steglitz: the telephone factory and the last vote
stops.date_confidence: relocation autumn 1932 attested; the dissolution vote is usually dated 20 July 1933 with formal closure in August 1933
stops.campa: Dessau withdraws the school's money under a National Socialist majority on its council. The Bauhaus rents a disused telephone factory on the Birkbuschstrasse in Berlin-Steglitz and keeps teaching there for two terms, in a building with no workshops worth the name. In the spring the Gestapo searches Paul Klee's house in Dessau; Klee is already dismissed and gone to Bern. In July the faculty votes to dissolve the school rather than accept the conditions offered, and in August it is closed.
suggested_refs: The former telephone factory at Birkbuschstrasse 49, Berlin-Steglitz

stops.name: Berlin: departure for a country neither has seen
stops.date_confidence: sailing date 18 November 1933 attested by Google's Doodle page; the port of departure is not named in any source reached, so the pin is Berlin, their last German ground
stops.campa: Philip Johnson, at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, is repeatedly credited with putting Josef Albers's name in front of the founders of a new college in the North Carolina mountains; the claim is standard and is not corroborated by the sources reached here. What is documented is the sailing. On the eighteenth of November the Alberses leave Germany for a country whose language Josef does not speak. Ninety-one years later Google will mark that date with a drawing, on the anniversary of the escape rather than of her birth.
suggested_refs: Google Doodle of 18 November 2024, marking the 1933 sailing

stops.name: Black Mountain College: arrival at Blue Ridge Assembly
stops.date_confidence: contested: English Wikipedia says November 1933, the Black Mountain College Museum says December 1933. Not resolved. Canonical Black Mountain pin inherited from merce_cunningham.journey.json and buckminster_fuller.journey.json
stops.campa: They reach Black Mountain College, three months old, housed in the rented buildings of the Blue Ridge Assembly south of the town: twenty-two students and a faculty that governs itself with no trustees and no grades. Josef is engaged to run the art program. Anni arrives without an appointment and works as an assistant, teaching a subject the college has no equipment for. The campus itself will move to the Lake Eden property in 1941, so her sixteen years there are spent on two different pieces of ground.
suggested_refs: Blue Ridge Assembly, Black Mountain, the college's rented campus 1933-1941
sources: Black Mountain College Museum and Arts Center

stops.name: Black Mountain College: faculty, and the grass instead of looms
stops.date_confidence: 1935 attested for the faculty appointment; month unknown and defaulted to January. The improvised-material teaching story is [R], recorded on Wikipedia as anecdote
stops.campa: She is made faculty and given weaving and textile design to teach. In the years when the college has no looms she sends students out for grasses, corn husks, pine needles and newspaper and has them build structures by hand until the equipment arrives. The story is told about her often enough to have become a teaching legend, and it is recorded here as one. Her own writing from these years argues that a craft is not a class of object but a way of coming at material, and that no material outranks another.
stops.quote: Weaving is an example of a craft which is many-sided. Besides surface qualities, such as rough and smooth, dull and shiny, hard and soft, it also includes color, and, as the dominating element, texture, which is the result of the construction of weaves. Like any craft it may end in producing useful objects, or it may rise to the level of art.
stops.quote_source: Anni Albers, 'Work with Material' (1937, first published Black Mountain College Bulletin 1938), in 'On Designing' / 'Selected Writings on Design', Wesleyan University Press, p. 9; read in a scan of the primary printing [A]
suggested_refs: Black Mountain College Bulletin, 'Work with Material', 1938
sources: Anni Albers, 'Selected Writings on Design' (Wesleyan), scan of p. 9

stops.name: Black Mountain College: the oath of citizenship
stops.date_confidence: contested: Wikipedia gives 1937, a secondary timeline gives 1939. Not resolved. Month unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: Josef and Anni Albers swear the citizenship of the country that took them, four years after the sailing. She is thirty-eight. Wikipedia dates the oath to 1937 and a secondary timeline to 1939, and the conflict is not resolved here. Behind them the school is dissolved by its own faculty vote and the Ullstein presses are in other hands. From this year her travelling goes south rather than east, and the weaving she studies is American and older than any loom in Europe.
suggested_refs: Naturalization records, Western District of North Carolina, 1937

stops.name: Mexico City: the first of the southern journeys
stops.date_confidence: [R] the 1935 first trip rests on a user-generated timeline; English Wikipedia dates her meeting with the backstrap loom to 1939, and the Guggenheim framing of roughly thirteen Latin American trips between 1935 and 1967 could not be retrieved
stops.campa: The Alberses go south into Mexico, the first of a long series of journeys that will carry them back roughly a dozen times over three decades. In the markets and the museums she meets weaving done without machines and with no line drawn between the useful and the sacred: pre-Columbian cloth built by counting threads. Josef photographs the pyramids. Anni buys textiles and small clay figures, and what they carry home becomes the reference library of both their teaching. The 1935 date rests on a user-made timeline and nothing firmer.
suggested_refs: The Albers collection of Mexican textiles and figures, Josef and Anni Albers Foundation

stops.name: Monte Alban: the flattened mountain above Oaxaca
stops.date_confidence: [R] the visit is widely repeated in Albers scholarship and no source reached fixes a year; the date is a placeholder inside the Mexico decade
stops.campa: On the levelled summit above Oaxaca the Zapotec city stands on terraces cut into the rock, its plazas squared off against the mountain. The visit is repeated throughout Albers scholarship and no source reached fixes a year for it. What she took from Oaxaca is visible afterwards in the cloth and is nowhere stated by her in these words. The Guggenheim's exhibition copy on the Albers travels in Latin America could not be retrieved for this account: the page returned a cookie banner and nothing else.
suggested_refs: Monte Alban, Oaxaca, Zapotec ceremonial centre
sources: General Albers scholarship, Guggenheim and Denver Art Museum programming (pages inaccessible)

stops.name: Mitla: the fretwork in stone
stops.date_confidence: [R] visit unattested to a year in anything reached; placeholder inside the Mexico decade
stops.campa: At Mitla the walls carry stone fretwork, thousands of cut blocks laid dry into step and meander patterns that a weaver reads at once: they are weaves, executed in rock. Critics have tied these walls to her later pictorial weavings ever since, and she never disowned the link. The visit itself cannot be dated from anything reached here. The step and the meander turn up in her weaving from 1936 onward, in thread rather than in stone. Whether the stone taught the cloth, or a weaver's eye found itself in the stone, is not settled by anything here.
suggested_refs: The fretwork palaces of Mitla, Oaxaca

stops.name: Black Mountain College: Ancient Writing on the loom
stops.date_confidence: the work is dated 1936; the claim that Mexico-derived weavings begin in that year rests only on a user timeline and is [R]
stops.campa: On the loom at Black Mountain she weaves Ancient Writing, a pictorial weaving whose field breaks into a script that spells nothing, the letters of a language she declines to invent. It is not a copy of a Mexican textile and not a picture of one. Eighty-two years later it will hang in Tate Modern as the opening argument of her first British retrospective. She is thirty-seven. The college has no money, and there is no market for a single object made on a loom.
stops.quote: And a longing for excitement can be satisfied without external means, within oneself; for creating is the most intense excitement one can come to know.
stops.quote_source: Anni Albers, 'Work with Material' (1937/38), in 'Selected Writings on Design', Wesleyan University Press, p. 8; read in a scan of the primary printing. Aggregator versions of this line alter the punctuation [A]
suggested_refs: Ancient Writing (1936), pictorial weaving, Smithsonian American Art Museum
sources: Anni Albers, 'Selected Writings on Design' (Wesleyan), scan of p. 8

stops.name: Willard Gallery, New York: necklaces of hardware
stops.date_confidence: attested: Anni Albers and Alex Reed, Exhibition of Necklaces, 5-25 May 1941. Accounts dating it 1940 are wrong; the December 1940 and December 1941 jewelry shows at Willard belong to Alexander Calder
stops.campa: At the Willard Gallery on East Fifty-seventh Street, Anni Albers and Alex Reed show necklaces made of hardware: sink strainers, paper clips, bobby pins, washers, corks and hair nets, assembled into collars that look like grave goods. The pieces began at Black Mountain out of the same logic as the grass exercises, which is that a material holds no rank of its own. The show runs from the fifth to the twenty-fifth of May and then travels. The gallery is one flight up, on a street of dealers in European painting.
suggested_refs: Willard Gallery, 32 East 57th Street, New York
Albers and Reed necklaces, Josef and Anni Albers Foundation

stops.name: Black Mountain College: the Harriet Engelhardt Memorial Collection
stops.date_confidence: conventionally 1947; Wikipedia gives no year, and the circulating range 1930s-1940s is impossible at its early end since the collection commemorates a student who died in the mid-1940s
stops.campa: With the college now on its own land at Lake Eden, Albers assembles a teaching collection of textiles in memory of Harriet Engelhardt, a student she advised who died in service abroad: cloth from Mexico and South America chiefly, with pieces from Italy, the Pacific islands and Africa. Students are meant to handle it, not to look at it through glass. No source reached gives the collection a founding year, and the range that circulates in the literature cannot be right at its early end.
suggested_refs: The Harriet Engelhardt Memorial Collection of textiles, Black Mountain College

stops.name: Black Mountain College: the summer of Cage, Cunningham and Fuller
stops.date_confidence: attested; canonical date and pin inherited byte-identical from merce_cunningham.journey.json and buckminster_fuller.journey.json
stops.campa: Josef Albers convenes a summer session and brings to the mountain John Cage, Merce Cunningham and Buckminster Fuller. Cage stages Erik Satie's Le Piege de Meduse with Fuller acting in it, and Fuller attempts his first dome on the campus lawn. Fuller had spent 1914 as an apprentice millwright in a Quebec textile mill, learning looms as machines. Anni Albers runs the weaving workshop through all of it, one year before she leaves the mountain for good.
suggested_refs: Black Mountain College summer session, 1948

stops.name: New York: the Museum of Modern Art gives a weaver the room
stops.date_confidence: 1949 attested; month unknown and defaulted to January. The tour of other American venues runs 1951-1953
stops.campa: The Museum of Modern Art gives her a solo exhibition, the first it has given any textile designer, and hangs weaving on walls it keeps for painting. The show travels to other American venues, touring from 1951 to 1953. For twenty-six years she has argued against the line between cloth that is used and objects that are looked at. The museum does not settle the question. It lends her its walls for two years and then takes them back. She is fifty years old and still teaching in Carolina.
stops.quote: there is no medium that cannot serve art.
stops.quote_source: Reported as a statement of her position in the Wikipedia article 'Anni Albers'; no essay or page cited in what could be retrieved, so treat as paraphrase risk rather than verbatim [R]
suggested_refs: Anni Albers Textiles, Museum of Modern Art, 1949

stops.name: Black Mountain College: the last term
stops.date_confidence: 1949 attested for the departure; month unknown, June chosen as the end of the academic year. Josef's Yale appointment is 1950, and accounts giving 1949 for Yale conflate the two
stops.campa: The Alberses leave Black Mountain after sixteen years, in a season when the college's politics have turned on its own faculty. She has taught weaving there since before it owned a loom. The college will last eight more years and close in 1957, and the Lake Eden campus will be sold off. She takes away her own weavings, the teaching collection of Mexican and Andean cloth she built for the students, and a stack of essays that will not reach a publisher for another ten years.
suggested_refs: Black Mountain College faculty records, 1949

stops.name: New Haven: the design department and the home studio
stops.date_confidence: 1950 attested for Josef's Yale appointment and the move; month unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: Josef Albers is made head of the Department of Design at Yale, a post he holds until he retires in 1958, and the couple move to New Haven. Anni Albers has no appointment at Yale and never holds a teaching post again. She is fifty-one. She weaves in a home studio, takes commissions for textiles in buildings, and writes: the essays that become On Designing and On Weaving are drafted in this house, over fifteen years, while her husband runs a department.
suggested_refs: Yale Department of Design under Josef Albers, 1950-1958

stops.name: Montville, Maine: the summer at Haystack
stops.date_confidence: summer 1950 attested; the pin is Montville township, where Haystack Mountain School of Crafts was founded that year. The school moved to Deer Isle only in 1961, so accounts placing this session at Deer Isle are wrong by ninety kilometres and eleven years
stops.campa: She teaches a summer session at the Haystack Mountain School of Crafts, founded that year on ground near Haystack Mountain in inland Maine. The school will move to the coast at Deer Isle only in 1961, so the many accounts that put this session on the island put it in a place that did not yet exist. The students in front of her are amateurs who came for a summer, not the picked intake of a Bauhaus, and she gives them the same material exercises she was given at Weimar.
suggested_refs: Haystack Mountain School of Crafts, Montville, Maine, founded 1950

stops.name: Lima: the collector in the capital
stops.date_confidence: [R] 1953-54 visiting professorships in Lima and Santiago are listed in a Josef Albers chronology and in a Foundation post; no month attested. Canonical Lima pin inherited from guaman_poma_de_ayala.journey.json
stops.campa: Josef Albers is invited to teach in Lima and Anni Albers goes with him, into the capital of the weaving tradition she has been studying from photographs and museum cases for fifteen years. She collects: fragments of Andean cloth, pieces small enough to carry home, structures worked in a technical vocabulary Europe never developed. It is the city to which Guaman Poma de Ayala carried his own record of the Andean world in 1615, hoping for a royal audience that never came.
suggested_refs: Instituto de Arte Contemporaneo, Lima
The Albers collection of Peruvian textile fragments
sources: Josef and Anni Albers Foundation post

stops.name: Cusco: the courses laid without mortar
stops.date_confidence: [R] the Peru trip is reported, a Cusco itinerary is not in anything reached; year taken from the Lima invitation
stops.campa: In the former Inca capital the walls are laid without mortar, every block cut to its neighbours so that no gap admits a blade. Her position in print is that structure comes before image, and Cusco is that position built at the scale of a city. The Peru journey is carried by the Albers Foundation's own materials and by a chronology of Josef's professorships. A specific Cusco itinerary is in nothing reached here, and the year given is the year of the Lima invitation, not of a dated arrival.
suggested_refs: Inca masonry of Cusco, Hatun Rumiyoc and the Qorikancha

stops.name: Machu Picchu: the terraces, on tradition
stops.date_confidence: [R] frequently asserted in popular and museum-adjacent accounts of the Albers Latin American travels; no primary itinerary confirms it
stops.campa: Tradition among her admirers puts the Alberses on the terraces of Machu Picchu, four decades after Bingham published the site and while the railway up the Urubamba is still a novelty. No itinerary in the sources reached confirms it, and the stop is kept here as tradition rather than as a visit. The country is the one whose weavers she names in print as her teachers. The terraces are cut in courses, one above another, up a ridge between two peaks.
suggested_refs: Machu Picchu, Urubamba valley
sources: Popular and museum-adjacent accounts of the Albers travels; no primary source found

stops.name: Paracas Peninsula: the necropolis of the weavers
stops.date_confidence: [R] the site is central to her writing and her presence on the ground is not established; the entry is kept as an inference from On Weaving, not as an attested visit
stops.campa: On the desert peninsula south of Pisco the Wari Kayan necropolis gave up hundreds of mummy bundles wrapped in embroidered mantles of a technical order unmatched in the ancient world, worked in wool and cotton by people with no writing and no wheel. Albers will call the weavers of ancient Peru her great teachers. Whether she walked this ground or knew it through collections and publications is not established here. The cloth reached her in fragments and photographs from the 1930s on; the desert, if she saw it at all, came later.
suggested_refs: The Wari Kayan necropolis at Cerro Colorado, Paracas
Paracas textiles, Museo Nacional de Arqueologia, Lima
sources: Metropolis, 'Looking Back at Anni Albers On Weaving, Five Decades Later'

stops.name: Santiago de Chile: the visiting chair
stops.date_confidence: [R] 1953-54 visiting professorship at the Universidad Catolica listed in a Josef Albers chronology; month unattested, June chosen to keep the South American circuit in order
stops.campa: Josef Albers holds a visiting professorship at the Universidad Catolica in Santiago, and the South American circuit closes on the far side of the Andes from the coast that mattered most to her. The Chile leg is carried by the Albers Foundation and by a chronology of his appointments and by nothing better; it is the least documented stop on this itinerary. She goes home with Andean cloth in her luggage, twelve years before On Weaving is dedicated to the weavers of ancient Peru.
suggested_refs: Universidad Catolica de Chile, Santiago
sources: Josef and Anni Albers Foundation post

stops.name: Cambridge, Massachusetts: Pictorial Weavings at MIT
stops.date_confidence: 1959 attested; month unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: An exhibition called Pictorial Weavings opens at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, an engineering school. The weavings shown are not designs for production. They are single objects made on a loom to be looked at, hung the way paintings are hung, in a building full of people who calculate structures for a living. Ten years earlier the Museum of Modern Art had hung her cloth on walls it keeps for painters. This time the room belongs to the engineers, and nobody in it has to be argued out of the word structure.
suggested_refs: Pictorial Weavings, MIT, 1959

stops.name: New Haven: On Designing, from Pellango Press
stops.date_confidence: 1959 attested for the Pellango Press edition, with Wesleyan taking it in 1962 and a paperback in 1971; month unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: On Designing appears from Pellango Press in New Haven, a collection of the essays she has been writing since Black Mountain. Wesleyan University Press takes it over in 1962 and issues a paperback in 1971. The prose is short-breathed and declarative, nearer to a workshop instruction than to criticism, and it holds one position throughout: material has intelligence, and design begins in obedience to it. She is sixty, and this is her first book. The essays in it were written for students who had no looms.
suggested_refs: Anni Albers, 'On Designing', Pellango Press, 1959

stops.name: New Haven: the Craftsmanship Medal
stops.date_confidence: 1961 attested; month unknown and defaulted to January. The pin is her residence, since no ceremony location is given in the sources reached
stops.campa: The American Institute of Architects gives her its Craftsmanship Medal. The award comes from the architects, not from the museums and not from the craft guilds, and it names what she has been doing since the cellophane wall covering at Bernau: solving problems of light and sound and surface inside buildings, on a loom, the way an engineer solves them. In 1981 the American Craft Council gives her its Gold Medal too, and by then she has not touched a loom for eleven years.
suggested_refs: AIA Craftsmanship Medal, 1961

stops.name: Hollywood: the Tamarind Lithography Workshop
stops.date_confidence: 1963 for the first invitation and 1964 for the fellowship and the portfolio Line Involvements, both attested; months unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: June Wayne invites her to the Tamarind Lithography Workshop on Tamarind Avenue in Hollywood, founded in 1960 to keep American lithography from dying out. Albers, who has been building lines out of thread for forty years, finds she can build them out of ink and build them faster. She returns the next year as a fellow and makes the portfolio Line Involvements. The loom is a slow machine and she is sixty-five; from here the graphic work expands and the weaving contracts.
suggested_refs: Line Involvements, portfolio of lithographs, Tamarind, 1964

stops.name: Middletown, Connecticut: On Weaving
stops.date_confidence: 1965 attested; month unknown and defaulted to January. The pin is the publisher, Wesleyan University Press
stops.campa: Wesleyan University Press publishes On Weaving: a book that sets Bauhaus structural diagrams beside photographs of pre-Columbian cloth and treats the two as one discipline. Its dedication names her teachers, and they are not the ones she had at Weimar. Her readers take the book as a rebuke to the Arts and Crafts hand-loom revival, the tradition William Morris and May Morris raised on the high-warp looms at Merton Abbey; the rebuke is drawn out by the readers more than stated by her. A 1966 review quoted by the Albers Foundation names no publication and is not reproduced here.
stops.quote: to my great teachers, the weavers of ancient Peru
stops.quote_source: Dedication, Anni Albers, 'On Weaving' (Wesleyan University Press, 1965), quoted on the Albers Foundation's On Weaving page and corroborated by Globalyell and Metropolis [A]
suggested_refs: Anni Albers, 'On Weaving', Wesleyan, 1965
David Zwirner Books expanded edition, 2017
sources: Josef and Anni Albers Foundation, 'On Weaving'

stops.name: Orange, Connecticut: the looms given away
stops.date_confidence: 1970 attested for the end of her loom work; month unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: She stops weaving and gives her looms away. She is seventy-one, she has printmaking, and she does not treat the change as a loss: the material has changed and the work follows the material, which is the position she has held in print since 1937. The threads that caught her against her will at Weimar in 1922 are let go after forty-eight years. She keeps making prints for another fourteen years, and the two books stay in circulation among weavers who never met her.
suggested_refs: Albers's late lithographs and screenprints, 1970-1984

stops.name: Bethany, Connecticut: the Foundation on Beacon Road
stops.date_confidence: 1971 attested for the founding; month unknown and defaulted to January. The Foundation's address is 88 Beacon Road, Bethany
stops.campa: Josef and Anni Albers found a foundation to hold both bodies of work, at Bethany on Beacon Road, north of New Haven. It will keep the archive, the collection of pre-Columbian textiles, the plates, and the estate after they are gone. They have no children. The institution is the heir. She is seventy-two. The school they came out of was dissolved in 1933 by a vote of its own faculty, in a rented Berlin factory; the Foundation is a trust and has no faculty to vote.
suggested_refs: Josef and Anni Albers Foundation, 88 Beacon Road, Bethany, Connecticut

stops.name: New Haven: the death of Josef Albers
stops.date_confidence: 1976 attested for the year of his death; no day or month is given in the sources reached, so both default to January
stops.campa: Josef Albers dies at eighty-eight, fifty-one years after the Dessau marriage and forty-three after the sailing. She is seventy-seven and has eighteen years of work in front of her. The obituaries treat him as one of the century's teachers of colour, and treat her, where they mention her at all, as his wife. She is a widow in her own studio at Orange, with the looms already six years gone. The exhibitions that will reverse that order are still ahead of her, and most of them are ahead of her death as well.
suggested_refs: Josef Albers, Homage to the Square series, 1950-1976

stops.name: Dusseldorf: the German exhibitions
stops.date_confidence: 1976 attested for major German exhibitions of her work; no venue-by-venue dating in the sources reached, and the pin is the Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen, her later German partner institution
stops.campa: Major exhibitions of her work open in Germany in the year her husband dies, forty-three years after the country expelled them both. The German rediscovery runs four decades ahead of the British one. The Bauhaus, dissolved by a vote in a rented factory in 1933, is by now a heritage industry with its own museums, and she is one of the few of its members still alive to be honoured by it. Whether she attends any of the openings is not recorded in anything reached here.
suggested_refs: Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen, Dusseldorf

stops.name: Washington: the Renwick retrospective
stops.date_confidence: 1985 attested; month unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: The Renwick Gallery mounts a retrospective. She is eighty-six. Four years earlier the American Craft Council gave her its Gold Medal, and the museums of the country that received her at thirty-four as an unpaid assistant have now fixed her position: a designer and a weaver, honoured in the craft wing of the national collection. The verdict of the following century, which will hang her among painters and call her one of the Bauhaus's major artists, is not yet in.
suggested_refs: Renwick Gallery retrospective, 1985
American Craft Council Gold Medal, 1981

stops.name: Orange, Connecticut: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested; the same 9 May that some sources wrongly graft onto her 1925 marriage
stops.campa: Anni Albers dies at home in Orange at ninety-four, in the year Connecticut inducts her into its Women's Hall of Fame. What became of her remains is recorded nowhere reached here: no burial, no cremation record, no marker. She had outlived the Bauhaus by sixty-one years and her husband by eighteen. The Foundation at Bethany holds the archive and the Andean cloth she carried home in fragments. Where the looms went when she gave them away in 1970 is not recorded either.
suggested_refs: Connecticut Women's Hall of Fame, class of 1994

stops.name: Tate Modern, London: three hundred and fifty objects
stops.date_confidence: attested; the exhibition ran 11 October 2018 to 27 January 2019, jointly with Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen
stops.campa: Tate Modern, with the Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen, opens the first major British exhibition of her work: over three hundred and fifty objects, many never shown in Britain, from Bauhaus samples to Ancient Writing of 1936 and the six-panel memorial weaving Six Prayers of 1966 and 1967. The student who was put into the weaving workshop instead of the glass workshop is twenty-four years dead. The museum builds rooms around her cloth and charges admission at the door.
suggested_refs: Anni Albers, Tate Modern, 11 October 2018 to 27 January 2019
Six Prayers (1966-67)
sources: Tate Modern exhibition page and press materials

stops.name: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston: the quipu comes north
stops.date_confidence: [R] adjacency, not a journey of hers; canonical pin and date inherited byte-identical from cecilia_vicuna.journey.json
stops.campa: Cecilia Vicuna's Disappeared Quipu travels to the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston in the same autumn as the Tate retrospective, into a museum that holds Andean cloth of its own. The quipu is the knotted record the Spanish burned and Guaman Poma de Ayala drew; Vicuna hangs it as storeys of unspun wool. Albers is twenty-four years dead. The line she asserted in 1965, from the Andean loom to the modern gallery, is by then being walked in the other direction, by a Chilean who came to the loom without her.
suggested_refs: Cecilia Vicuna, Disappeared Quipu, Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 2018
